slides.body: There are six steps, and their order matters more than the tools.
Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
Three words first. A secret here is a credential, such as an API key: a string that proves to a service who is asking.
Two sections. Section 21B.14: responding to a leaked secret in six steps: contain, assess, eradicate, recover, communicate, prevent.
One note on the names. The textbook says the names of the phases follow common incident-response practice.
The demonstration replays the first three steps of the tabletop lab, a rehearsal of an incident with nothing real at stake.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.direction: The table of section 21B.14, one step at a time.
header: Evidence of what goes wrong otherwise
rows: Revoke or rotate the credential first. That alone may be sufficient, and a history rewrite may not be warranted (GitHub, OWASP)

an xAI key valid about two months after the first alert; a contractor's AWS keys valid 48 hours after the repository was taken down (Krebs on Security); the Internet Archive breached a second time through tokens it had not rotated (BleepingComputer)

Identify the secret, its owner and what it can reach; check validity status and exposure labels; review GitHub audit logs and the provider's logs for use; include forks, deleted forks and force-pushed commits in scope (remediation guide)
an affected company declined to say whether logs showed third-party use of an exposed token (TechCrunch)

Remove the secret from current code; rewrite history only where warranted, with git-filter-repo 2.47 or later, then force-push, then a GitHub Support request. Support assists only where rotation cannot mitigate the risk (GitHub)
after a supply-chain compromise the scope is every credential reachable from the affected runtime (CISA)

slides.direction: The table of section 21B.14, one step at a time.
header: Evidence of what goes wrong otherwise
rows: Update dependent services with the new credential; if history was rewritten, have collaborators re-clone and re-enable force-push protection; close the alert as revoked and document
partial rotation produced a second breach (Internet Archive)
Track internally; tell collaborators exactly what to do with their clones; keep a reachable disclosure contact such as SECURITY.md
a researcher could not find a way to report a contractor's leak and went to the press (Cybersecurity Dive); concealment turned Uber's 2016 breach into a regulatory case (FTC)

Push protection; pre-commit and CI scanning; secrets out of code; short-lived credentials through OIDC; least privilege; staging named files and reviewing git diff --cached instead of git add .; scheduled rotation
hardcoded long-lived keys recur in every case of section 21B.15

Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Starting with the repository. Root cause: the damage happens at the issuer, where the key is accepted; until revocation the key works for whoever copied it.

Rewriting history by reflex. Root cause: for a revoked key the rewrite removes nothing that still matters, and it costs every collaborator their clone, invalidates recorded commit IDs and strips signatures.
Rotating one credential after a runtime was compromised. Root cause: the scope is every credential reachable from that runtime; partial rotation is how a second breach happens.
Reporting "we found no use" from Git or from GitHub alone. Root cause: whether the key was used is recorded at the issuer; Git answers only which commits and which refs.

items: The six steps are contain, assess, eradicate, recover, communicate, prevent, and the order matters more than the tools.
Revocation comes first because the damage happens at the issuer, and it is the only step that works against every copy; it may be all that is needed.

An assessment produces five facts: the secret and its reach, the first commit and first push, the refs, who could read it, and whether it was used; Git answers the second and third, and only the issuer answers the last.
Rewrite history when the data stays harmful after rotation or cannot be rotated, not by reflex for a revoked key; record the decision.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Starting with the repository. Root cause: the damage happens at the issuer, where the key is accepted; until revocation the key works for whoever copied it.
beats.tele: Starting with the repository. Root cause: the damage happens at the issuer, where the key is accepted; until revocation the key works for whoever copied it.

beats.text: Rewriting history by reflex. Root cause: for a revoked key the rewrite removes nothing that still matters, and it costs every collaborator their clone, invalidates recorded commit IDs and strips signatures.
beats.tele: Rewriting history by reflex. Root cause: for a revoked key the rewrite removes nothing that still matters, and it costs every collaborator their clone, invalidates recorded commit IDs and strips signatures.

beats.text: Rotating one credential after a runtime was compromised. Root cause: the scope is every credential reachable from that runtime; partial rotation is how a second breach happens.
beats.tele: Rotating one credential after a runtime was compromised. Root cause: the scope is every credential reachable from that runtime; partial rotation is how a second breach happens.

beats.text: Reporting "we found no use" from Git or from GitHub alone. Root cause: whether the key was used is recorded at the issuer; Git answers only which commits and which refs.
